summary: This best current practice sets out procedures for handling harassment at IETF meetings, virtual meetings, social events and on mailing lists. It defines how complaints are managed and enforced, and updates RFC 2418 with new working group guidelines and procedures.

eli5.summary: Everyone at IETF meetings should be treated kindly. This sets out what happens if someone is not, and who deals with it.

questions: how does the ietf handle harassment
how do i report harassment at an ietf meeting
what remedies can the ietf impose for harassment
how does the ietf harassment appeal work
subtitle: How the IETF receives, investigates and acts on reports of harassment, through a small appointed team called the Ombudsteam.

tldr.problem: Personal harassment at IETF meetings, social events and on mailing lists does not disrupt working group progress directly, so the existing rules for disruptive behavior do not handle it well.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF Chair appoints an Ombudsteam of at least three people. It takes confidential reports, investigates only with the agreement of the people involved, and can impose remedies from a private plan up to removal from IETF activities, with a defined appeal path.
tldr.outcome: The IETF has a confidential, documented process with remedies, conflict-of-interest rules and an appeal route. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 8716.

today: RFC 7776 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8716. It updates RFC 2418 and RFC 7437.

sections.title: Why a Separate Procedure
sections.content:
The IETF already had guidelines for personal interaction (RFC 7154) and for disruptive behavior in working group meetings and on mailing lists (RFC 2418 and RFC 3934). Some problematic behavior is more personal and does not directly disrupt a working group, yet is still unacceptable between participants.

This document sets out procedures for that behavior. They are meant to be used when other IETF policies and procedures do not apply or have been ineffective. Nothing in the document interferes with the due process of law or releases anyone from contractual or corporate policies.
sections.eli5: The old rules were about people who make meetings hard to run. This new set is for people who are unkind to other people, which needs its own careful plan.

sections.title: Definitions and What Counts as Harassment
sections.content:
The RFC defines the roles: a Reporter reports potential harassment, a Respondent is claimed to have harassed, and a Subject is the person, group or class the behavior was directed at. The Ombudsteam takes and evaluates reports and imposes actions or remedies. An Ombudsperson is a member of it, and the Lead Ombudsperson is the primary contact for one report.

It adopts the IESG's general definition: unwelcome hostile or intimidating behavior, in particular speech or behavior that is sexually aggressive or intimidates based on attributes such as race, gender, religion, age, color, national origin, ancestry, disability, sexual orientation, or gender identity. It does not try to define the behavior more precisely or list every attribute.

Disruption on a working group or general mailing list, or at a working group or plenary meeting, can normally be dealt with by the usual procedures. Harassment fits these procedures better, and any definition of harassment prohibited by applicable law can be handled here.
sections.eli5: It gives names to everyone in the story, like the person who tells, the person accused and the person it happened to. It says harassment is hostile or scary behavior that nobody wanted.

sections.title: The Ombudsteam
sections.content:
The Ombudsteam has no fewer than three people and is appointed solely by the IETF Chair, who may consult the community, solicit nominations, and appoint more than three. The Chair is encouraged to appoint at least some members from within the IETF community.

An Ombudsperson serves a two-year term, extended until a report they lead is finished. The Chair decides on reappointment and may remove an Ombudsperson before the end of the term without explanation to the community. Removal can be appealed to the IESG as a whole.

Ombudspersons receive no compensation, including meeting fees, pay for time, expenses and travel. The IETF does fund training and external legal and HR advice through the IASA.
sections.eli5: A small group of trusted helpers is picked by the head of the IETF. They volunteer for two years at a time and are not paid, but they get training and expert advice.

sections.title: Handling a Report
sections.content:
Any participant who believes they or anyone else has been harassed should tell any serving Ombudsperson, by email to ombuds@ietf.org or directly. The Ombudsteam also gives confidential advice to anyone unsure about behavior. It will not start a formal investigation without agreement by the Reporter and Subject.

One Ombudsperson becomes the Lead Ombudsperson for the report. The Lead discusses events with the Reporter, may advise on handling the matter alone, or may point to regular IETF procedures for disruptive behavior. Otherwise, with the Subject's agreement to proceed (the Reporter's if there is no individual Subject), the team may investigate and impose a remedy. The Subject can withdraw agreement at any time.

The team must document its operating practices, discuss them with the IESG and publish them. Required components include coverage of every IETF meeting by at least one Ombudsperson, strict confidentiality as far as possible, contacting the Respondent before imposing a remedy, a timely investigation, written results, secure written records, and protection from retaliation for good faith reports or cooperation. The Respondent is not obliged to cooperate, but the team may consider a refusal when choosing a remedy.
sections.eli5: If someone is being treated badly, they can tell one of the helpers. The helper listens, gives advice and keeps it private, and only looks into it formally if the people involved agree.

sections.title: Remedies
sections.content:
After examining a complaint, the Ombudsteam prepares a brief summary and discusses it with all parties, aiming for agreement. If it finds harassment took place, it decides the next action. That may be passing the matter to normal procedures through a WG Chair or IESG member, a plan with the Respondent so it does not recur, or mediation if both parties agree. At the other end it may bar the Respondent from a particular IETF activity, such as ejecting them from a meeting or stopping them from attending future meetings.

The team has ultimate responsibility for the choice of remedy and is expected to apply proportionality and reasonableness. Where a remedy is removal from activities, the Lead tells the Secretariat in writing, disclosing only the remedy and not the nature of the harassment.

The purpose is to stop escalation and repeat incidents, not retribution. Because the process is confidential, a remedy cannot itself serve as a deterrent or teach the community, but knowing that a range of remedies exists is a deterrent.
sections.eli5: The helpers can pick anything from a friendly chat to asking someone to leave a meeting. The aim is to make it stop, not to punish.

sections.title: Remedies for People in IETF Positions
sections.content:
The Ombudsteam cannot itself remove someone from an IETF management position, but it can use existing mechanisms. For NomCom-appointed positions, this document updates RFC 7437 so the Ombudsteam can form a recall petition on its own, without the 20 signatories otherwise required. For positions filled by the IESG, IAB, ISOC Board or ISOC President, it may recommend removal to the appointing body. For positions filled by an AD, or by WG Chairs, it makes a written recommendation to the AD.

Recipients are expected to take the recommendation extremely seriously and not to reinvestigate. Removal is an act of last resort, and the Respondent should first be given ample opportunity to step down. If an AD declines to follow a recommendation, the Ombudsteam raises it with the whole IESG, which may reorganize responsibilities so that the AD is no longer in the direct management path.
sections.eli5: Some people have important jobs in the IETF. The helpers cannot fire them, but they can ask the people who gave out the job to do it, and those people are expected to listen.

sections.title: Appeals, Conflicts and Confidentiality
sections.content:
A dissatisfied Subject, Reporter or Respondent first talks to the Lead Ombudsperson, then the IETF Chair. If that fails, the decision can be formally appealed, strictly on whether the Ombudsteam exercised due diligence, not to re-investigate or negotiate the remedy. An Appeals Group of the IETF Chair (or a delegated IESG member) and two other IESG members decides, within 24 hours when the impact is immediate and tied to an ongoing meeting. Its decision on due diligence is final. The only further recourse is to claim the procedures themselves are inadequate, in an appeal to the Internet Society Board of Trustees.

Anyone with a conflict of interest, such as being a party to the matter or closely associated with one, is expected to recuse, meaning to step out completely. If the IETF Chair is involved in an appeal, the IESG picks a replacement.

Confidentiality protects Reporters, Subjects, Respondents and witnesses. The community is asked to show restraint and trust the Ombudsteam.
sections.eli5: If someone thinks the helpers got it wrong, they can ask a small panel to check that the helpers did their job carefully. Anyone who knows the people involved has to step aside, and everyone keeps it private.
